name: Raw milk

card.summary: Unpasteurized milk, pushed in some circles for height, skin and 'primal' health; reviews find little nutritional gain from skipping pasteurization and documented infection risks.
card.aka: Unpasteurized milk, farm-fresh milk, primal diet milk
card.note: Health agencies document outbreaks of Listeria, Salmonella, E. coli and Campylobacter linked to raw milk; sale is restricted or banned in many places.

quick.overview:
Raw milk is milk that has not been heated (pasteurized) to kill microbes. In looksmaxxing and 'primal diet' circles it is promoted as a more nutrient-dense, enzyme-rich food that some say supports skin, hormones, digestion and, for the young, height.

A 2011 systematic review found that pasteurization changes some vitamin levels slightly and that its effect on nutritive value is minimal, and it found no good evidence for claims about allergy, cancer or lactose intolerance. Other forum members argue that raw milk cannot change bone structure after growth plates fuse, and some call the practice 'cope'.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say heat destroys enzymes, immunoglobulins, vitamins and beneficial bacteria, so unheated milk keeps more of them active. Pasteurization is designed to reduce viable pathogens; the review literature reports measurable reductions in some water-soluble vitamins (B1, B2, C, folate) but small overall nutritional effect.
quick.risks: Raw milk can carry pathogens such as Listeria, Salmonella, E. coli and Campylobacter, and pregnant women, children, older adults and immunocompromised people are at greatest risk of serious illness. Legal status varies: some places ban retail sale, others allow farm sales with labels. Forum members also report acne or bloating, and some discuss large intakes for body-composition goals.

lead: Raw milk, also called unpasteurized milk, is milk from cows, goats, sheep or other animals that has not been heat-treated to reduce microbes. In appearance-focused communities it is discussed as part of 'primal' or carnivore-style eating. Proponents say a whole, unheated dairy food supplies nutrients, protein and fat that support skin quality, lean mass, digestion and hormones, and, for adolescents who are still growing, height.[1][10]

The modern raw-milk movement has identifiable roots: the Weston A. Price Foundation, founded in 1999, campaigns for legal access to unpasteurized milk, and the late Aajonus Vonderplanitz built a raw-animal-food 'Primal Diet' around raw milk, raw meat and raw eggs, which he trademarked in 2000.[16][17] Looksmaxxing forums borrow from both traditions and add their own goals, such as skin clarity, a leaner jawline and facial development.[10][11]

A 2011 systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 studies found that pasteurization lowered vitamins B1, B2, C and folate, raised or left others unchanged, and had minimal effect on the milk's overall nutritive value; it also found no sound evidence that raw milk prevents or treats allergies, cancer or lactose intolerance.[3] The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the FDA recommend pasteurized milk, and public-health literature links raw milk to infections including listeriosis, brucellosis, salmonellosis and tick-borne encephalitis.[5][6][7][8][15] Legal rules differ widely by country and US state.[1]
infobox: Interstate sale for human consumption banned since 1987; 43 states allow some sales [1]
CDC advises pasteurized milk; higher-risk groups include children under 5, adults over 65, pregnant women, immunocompromised people [15]

paras: Raw milk is milk that has not been pasteurized, a heating process that reduces the number of viable pathogenic bacteria and extends shelf life.[1][3] Wikipedia notes that raw milk typically keeps for only about three to five days refrigerated.[1] Some traditional cheeses are made from raw milk, and fermented products such as kefir are made from milk with grains of yeasts and bacteria; these are separate products from drinking raw milk itself.[1][9]

Raw milk contains a complex community of microorganisms that enter from the udder, the environment and equipment. Reviews describe some as useful for dairy fermentation or associated with health (lactobacilli, bifidobacteria) and others as spoilage organisms or pathogens such as Listeria, Salmonella, E. coli and Campylobacter.[2] Wikipedia cites a Cornell survey that found pathogens in between 0.87 and 12.6 percent of raw milk samples, depending on the study.[1]

sections.h: How people use it for their looks
paras: In looksmaxxing and primal-diet circles raw milk is usually drunk fresh from a farm source as one part of an animal-food-centred diet that may also include raw eggs, liver and other meats. Users describe a handful of appearance goals: clearer skin, a better body composition from calorie-dense dairy protein and fat, improved digestion and less bloating, and, for people still in their teens, growth in height.[10][11]

Some posters link raw milk to facial structure, hoping a 'primal' diet will support bone and soft-tissue development; other members of the same forums reply that bone growth is fixed once growth plates fuse.[11] The practice is typically presented as a long-term dietary habit rather than a short protocol, and users report their own results rather than measured outcomes.[10]

Dairy animals were domesticated roughly 9000 to 7000 BC in Mesopotamia, and for most of history milk was consumed unheated.[1] Louis Pasteur developed pasteurization in 1864, and the process was introduced in the United States in the 1890s.[1]

According to Wikipedia, before pasteurization an estimated 10 percent of human tuberculosis cases were attributed to milk, and milk accounted for about a quarter of food and waterborne outbreaks in the US before World War II versus under 1 percent now, which authors attribute largely to pasteurization.[1] The CDC likewise says pasteurization, used since the early 1900s, greatly reduced milk-borne illness.[15]
Regulation followed in many places, for example the US ban on interstate sale for human consumption in 1987 and Canada's prohibition of direct sales in 1991.[1]

The Weston A. Price Foundation was co-founded in 1999 by Sally Fallon Morell and nutritionist Mary Enig and advocates for removing rules that require milk pasteurization so raw milk can be bought legally in every US state. In July 2007 the foundation helped establish the Farm-to-Consumer Legal Defense Fund, which supports farmers who sell raw dairy and other foods directly to consumers.[17] Its supporters argue that pasteurization harms beneficial components of milk.[17]

The CDC and FDA disagree with this position; in 2010 an FDA dairy-safety director called the group's raw-milk claims 'false, devoid of scientific support, and misleading to consumers,' according to Wikipedia. Critics, including writers in Science-Based Medicine and Quackwatch, have also objected to the foundation's wider dietary positions.[17]

Aajonus Vonderplanitz (1947-2013) promoted a diet of raw meat, eggs, dairy and fats that he trademarked as the Primal Diet in 2000, and described it in books including We Want to Live (1997; second edition 2005) and The Recipe for Living Without Disease (2002).[16] Wikipedia reports that in 2001 his report and the threat of legal action helped persuade Los Angeles County's board of supervisors to end its ban on retail raw milk sales, and that he developed 'animal leasing,' in which a private food club leases a dairy farm.[16] His Right to Choose Healthy Food organization grew to about 80 food clubs by 2010.[16]

Vonderplanitz also made claims that his protocols cured cancer, which mainstream medical scientists have not tested, and the Rawesome food club in Los Angeles was raided on 30 June 2010 and closed after a second raid in August 2011.[16] He died in Thailand in August 2013 after a fall.[16]

Advocacy groups describe raw milk as a more complete food, claiming that heat destroys vitamins and enzymes and that raw milk can help with allergies, cancer and lactose intolerance.[3][17] Wikipedia notes US proponents also say pasteurization kills beneficial bacteria, a point the FDA disputes.[1] In looksmaxxing forums, posters echo this, adding claims about skin, hormones, gut health and, for young people, growth hormone and height.[10]
Other members argue the opposite: one thread contends that raw milk and raw-meat 'primal' diets cannot reshape facial bone structure once growth plates have fused, calling such hopes 'cope.'[11]

The 2011 meta-analysis reported decreases in some vitamins after pasteurization (B1, B2, C, folate), no significant effect on B6, and an increase in vitamin A, concluding that the effect on nutritive value was minimal.[3] The CDC states that pasteurized milk offers the same nutritional benefits without the risks.[15]

Studies in children raised on farms have associated raw milk with fewer allergies and asthma, but, as Wikipedia notes, the protective effect may reflect the farm environment in general rather than the milk; a review concluded that most such studies did not confirm raw-milk status or compare with heat-treated milk.[1] A letter on a randomized trial asked whether yoghurt could be an acceptable alternative to raw milk for reducing infant eczema and allergy.[12]
Pasteurized milk is not risk-free: a 1983 Massachusetts listeriosis outbreak was traced to a brand of pasteurized milk.[13]

The CDC lists Campylobacter, Cryptosporidium, E. coli, Listeria, Brucella and Salmonella among the organisms that raw milk products can carry, and names children under 5, adults over 65, pregnant women and people with weakened immune systems as being at higher risk of serious illness. Symptoms include diarrhea, cramping and vomiting; severe outcomes include Guillain-Barre syndrome and hemolytic uremic syndrome.[15]

Wikipedia cites 144 raw-milk-linked outbreaks in the US from 2007 to 2016, and reports that a 2015 case in Australia involved the death of a four-year-old from hemolytic uremic syndrome after drinking raw milk.[1] Other infections associated with raw milk or raw dairy include listeriosis (especially from soft raw-milk cheeses), brucellosis, tick-borne encephalitis and Q fever.[5][6][7][8][14]

During the 2024 US H5N1 outbreak in dairy cattle, a study found influenza A virus could survive in refrigerated raw milk, and the CDC advised against drinking raw milk contaminated with H5N1 in an attempt to build antibodies.[1][15] Forum posters themselves list bacterial risk from poor sources, acne and bloating among the downsides.[10]

Wikipedia summarizes regional rules. In the US the FDA has banned interstate sale since 1987 and 43 states allow some form of raw milk sales; Canada has prohibited direct sales since 1991; Australia has banned drinking-milk sales since the 1940s, with 'bath milk' sold as a workaround; Brazil has banned sales since 1969; and in the UK about 150 producers are listed in England, Wales and Northern Ireland while Scotland has restricted sales since 1983.[1]

In the EU member states may prohibit or restrict sales and must label raw-milk products; Norway, Sweden and Denmark do not allow shop sales while Finland allows packaged sales, and Germany licensed about 80 farmers as of 2012 to sell packaged raw milk as 'Vorzugsmilch.'[1] Kenya reported that 85 percent of milk was consumed raw in 2018.[1]

Raw milk sits alongside other animal-food-focused approaches discussed in the same communities, including carnivore-style eating and raw-egg and liver consumption, and alongside fermented dairy such as kefir.[9][11]

No studies found of raw milk for appearance, skin or height. Related human research includes a randomized pilot study of raw milk and lactose intolerance and a 2011 meta-analysis of pasteurization and vitamin content.[3][4]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, raw milk appears in threads about primal diets, height, skin and testosterone, with some users enthusiastic and others dismissive.[10][11]

claims.claim: Raw milk keeps more vitamins and enzymes than pasteurized milk
claims.believers: Proponents say heat destroys enzymes and reduces vitamins A, C, E and B, so raw milk is more nutritious.[10]
claims.experts: A systematic review found some vitamins fell (B1, B2, C, folate), vitamin A rose, and overall nutritive effect was minimal.[3]

claims.claim: Raw milk helps height or growth in young people
claims.believers: One poster suggests raw milk's hormones may help height if consumed while young.[10]
claims.experts: No published studies were found testing raw milk for height or facial growth; the cited review covers vitamins, allergy, cancer and lactose intolerance only.[3]

claims.claim: Raw milk improves digestion and lactose tolerance
claims.believers: Users say enzymes and immunoglobulins make raw milk easier to digest and that they feel less bloated.[10]
claims.experts: A randomized pilot study of raw milk for lactose intolerance did not show it to be better tolerated, and the meta-analysis found no good evidence for the claim.[3][4]

claims.claim: Raw milk eases allergies, asthma and autoimmune problems
claims.believers: A poster reports that asthma symptoms improved and says raw milk keeps the immune system balanced.[10]
claims.experts: Farm-child studies link raw milk with fewer allergies, but reviewers note the effect may stem from the farm environment; the meta-analysis found no sound evidence for treating allergy.[1][3]

claims.claim: Raw milk and raw meat can remodel facial bones
claims.believers: Some posters on primal diets hope raw milk and liver will deepen eye sockets or strengthen cheekbones.[11]
claims.experts: Other forum users note that growth plates fuse in the late teens and that diet is not known to create new midface bone; no studies have tested the claim.[11]

claims.claim: Raw milk is safe if sourced well
claims.believers: Posters acknowledge bacterial risk 'if from bad source' while presenting well-sourced milk as acceptable.[10]
claims.experts: Public-health reviews document outbreaks and serious illness, especially in pregnant, young, elderly and immunocompromised people.[1][7][8]

claims.claim: Raw milk is part of a 'primal' diet that builds a better body and skin
claims.believers: Followers of the Primal Diet tradition describe raw dairy, meat and eggs as a complete, unprocessed diet.[16]
claims.experts: Vonderplanitz's cancer-cure claims were never tested by mainstream scientists, and no published trial has tested the Primal Diet for appearance outcomes.[16]

claims.claim: Pasteurization is unnecessary if the farm is clean
claims.believers: The Weston A. Price Foundation says raw milk can be produced hygienically.[17]
claims.experts: The CDC and FDA recommend pasteurized milk, and Wikipedia reports 144 US outbreaks linked to raw milk from 2007 to 2016.[1][15]

angle.text: People who drink raw milk for their looks do so as a nutrient-dense whole food, expecting better skin, body composition and, if young, height. Published studies of raw milk have examined vitamins, allergy and lactose tolerance rather than appearance outcomes.
